passage: Devika, you asked why I keep the old group chat but never post. I'm Wasim, and at fifteen I felt invisible at home. Abba worked nights and nobody asked about my day. Then an online community began greeting me by name every morning and saying they were glad I was there. That warmth was real, and I won't pretend it wasn't. I nearly moved my whole life into it. But one night I asked myself: does being welcome make everything they teach true? I couldn't say yes. So I joined the school cricket club, made two friends who could sit beside me, and kept the chat as one small part of my days.

qa.q: How old was Wasim when the online community began greeting Wasim by name?
What was Wasim feeling at home, and why did the community appeal?
qa.a: Wasim felt invisible at home, so a community greeting Wasim by name every morning felt warm and welcome. 🙂

qa.q: What offline step did Wasim take?
qa.a: Wasim joined the school cricket club and made two friends who could sit beside Wasim, keeping the chat as one small part of life.

qa.q: What would probably have been different if Wasim had felt seen at home?
qa.a: The pull of an online welcome would likely have been weaker, since Wasim would not have felt so invisible.

grounding: Wasim feels unseen at home and is warmly welcomed by an online community, finds the warmth real but not proof of truth, and builds offline friendships.

passage:
It was the week of the half-yearly exams, the power kept cutting out, and at home in Hyderabad nobody seemed to see Yusuf at all. His baby sister had colic; his parents moved around the flat like ghosts, holding her.

But every night, on his phone's last bit of battery, the online group for the young preacher was there. "Yusuf! Brother, how was your day?" Thirty people knew his name. They sent voice notes. They prayed for his exams. He felt warm for the first time in weeks.

On Wednesday, a group admin wrote, "The people around you don't understand you like we do." Yusuf paused. They were kind. But was kindness the same as being right?

At school the next day, Siddharth, who sat behind him, asked if he wanted to come to chess club after exams. Yusuf almost said no. Then he said yes.

That weekend, with the lights finally back on, he played three games and lost all of them. He laughed anyway.

qa.q: What did the group admin write on Wednesday?
qa.a: The admin wrote, "The people around you don't understand you like we do."

qa.q: What did Yusuf feel when the group greeted him every night?
qa.a: Yusuf felt warm and seen for the first time in weeks, because at home he felt invisible.

qa.q: Why was saying yes to chess club a good choice?
qa.a: It gave Yusuf real, offline friends, so the online group was not his only source of warmth and belonging.

qa.q: How might Yusuf's parents feel if they knew how unseen he felt?
qa.a: They would probably feel sad and a bit guilty, since they love him but were exhausted caring for the baby.

grounding: It shows a teen who feels unseen at home and is warmly welcomed by an online preacher's community, noticing that warmth is not proof of truth and building offline friendships.

passage:
Nitin's parents both worked night shifts at the textile mill in Surat, so most evenings he ate alone in front of the TV. Then he found the live chat on a preacher's channel.

"Welcome back, Nitin bhai!" someone typed every night at nine. They asked about his day, remembered his maths test, sent him blessings. It felt like a big family.

After a month, the messages changed a little. "Bring your friends. Share the channel. Real family is here, not outside." Nitin felt a small itch. His real family was at the mill, working for him.

On Sunday, Shankar, the older boy from the second floor, knocked. "We're short one for cricket in the lane. You in?"

Nitin went. He was out for four runs. Shankar's mother gave everyone lemon water. On the way back up, Shankar said, "Come every Sunday."

That night Nitin still opened the chat. It was still warm. But he didn't share the channel, and he wrote "cricket 7am" on his calendar.

qa.q: Where did Nitin's parents work night shifts?
qa.a: They worked night shifts at the textile mill in Surat.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling when the chat started saying real family was there, not outside?
qa.a: Nitin felt a small itch of unease, because his real family was working for him at the mill.

qa.q: What did Nitin do that balanced the online warmth?
qa.a: Nitin joined Sunday cricket with Shankar and did not share the channel, building offline friendships while noticing the group's pull.

qa.q: How might Shankar see Nitin joining the game?
qa.a: Shankar seems glad to have Nitin, inviting him to come every Sunday and probably noticing he was often alone.

grounding: It shows a teen who feels unseen at home and finds real warmth in an online preacher's community, noticing that warmth is not proof and building offline friendships.
